newsitem.title: USA: Denver surprised by SEC silence on airport probe.
newsitem.headline: Denver surprised by SEC silence on airport probe.

text.p: Denver City Attorney Daniel Muse said Wednesday he is "flabbergasted" that SEC has yet to notify the city of its findings in its two-year-old probe of Denver airport bonds in light of press reports that it plans to drop the case.

"I'm flabbergasted," Daniel Muse said in a telephone interview. "Everyone seems to know that they are going to close down the investigation against the city of Denver, except the city of Denver," he said.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the Securities and Exchange Commission is expected to end its long-term probe of municipal bonds sold to finance Denver's new $4.9 billion airport without taking any enforcement action.

William McLucas, SEC director of enforcement, and Paul Maco, head of SEC's office of municipal securities, said they could not comment on the Journal story. Daniel Shea, director of SEC's central regional office in Denver, was unavailable for comment.
Muse told Reuters, "It seems to me that the targets of the investigation should be the first to know rather than the last."
He said he stands by his "longstanding position that there never was a valid basis for serious consideration of the city for violation of the securities laws."

He said SEC's own rules say that an issuer can make "forward looking statements" about a project without the threat of a securities fraud violation as long as there was a "reasonable basis" for those projections.
That is the case "even if those projections turn out to be wrong," Muse added.
Attorneys for bond underwriting firms involved in the probe also said they could not comment.

SEC's Denver office notified the city last October that it plans to recommend SEC bring an "administrative action" against the city for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.

SEC's Denver staff alleged the city failed to disclose to bond investors potential problems with a state-of-the-art baggage system that led to a 16-month delay in opening the facility and ballooning costs.
The city disputed the staff charges in a 20-page letter on Dec 7, claiming Congress did not intend federal securities fraud charges to apply to state and local issuers.
